tracks.name: Node.js Core
tracks.description: The Node.js runtime, process object, built-in modules, and the file system.

lessons.title: 1. What is Node.js?
lessons.summary: JavaScript runs outside the browser — here's how.

activities.title: JavaScript beyond the browser
activities.instruction: Node.js is a runtime that lets you run JavaScript on your computer instead of in a browser. You write `.js` files and run them with the `node` command.

activities.title: What runs this code?
activities.question: Where does `console.log('Hi')` run when you type `node hello.js` in the terminal?
choices: In the Node.js runtime on your computer
activities.answer: In the Node.js runtime on your computer
activities.explanation: Node.js executes JavaScript directly on your machine using the V8 engine — no browser needed.

activities.title: Print your first Node.js message
activities.instruction: Print exactly: Hello from Node.js!

teaching.text: Node.js takes JavaScript out of the browser. Instead of writing code that runs in Chrome or Firefox, you write `.js` files and run them with the `node` command from your terminal.
Under the hood, Node.js uses Google's V8 engine — the same engine Chrome uses. But instead of `window` and `document`, you get `process`, `Buffer`, and access to the file system.
Node.js is great for servers, command-line tools, and scripts — anything that doesn't need a browser.

hints: Use `console.log()` with the message in quotes.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What's the difference between running JavaScript in a browser versus running it with Node.js?

lessons.title: 2. The process object
lessons.summary: Access information about the running program and the system.

activities.title: Reading system info
activities.instruction: The global `process` object gives you info about the current Node.js process — the Node version, platform, memory usage, and command-line arguments.

activities.title: What is process.version?
activities.question: What does `process.version` return?
choices: The version of the file you're running
The version of your operating system
activities.explanation: process.version returns the Node.js version string, like 'v20.11.0'.

activities.title: Print the Node.js version
activities.instruction: Print the Node.js version using process.version.

teaching.text: `process` is a global object in Node.js — you can use it anywhere without importing it. It tells you about the current running program.
`process.version` returns the Node.js version. `process.platform` tells you the OS (`win32`, `darwin`, `linux`). `process.memoryUsage()` shows how much memory the program is using.
You can also read command-line arguments from `process.argv` — an array of strings the user passed when running the script.

lessons.task: Print the Node.js version using process.version.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why is process a global object instead of something you have to import?

lessons.title: 3. Command-line arguments
lessons.summary: Accept input from the terminal when running a script.

activities.title: Reading arguments
activities.instruction: `process.argv` is an array. The first two elements are the Node executable and the script path. Everything after that is user-provided input.

activities.title: Which index?
activities.question: If you run `node app.js banana`, what is `process.argv[2]`?
activities.explanation: process.argv[0] is 'node', process.argv[1] is 'app.js', and process.argv[2] is the first user argument 'banana'.

activities.title: Echo the first argument
activities.instruction: Print whatever argument is passed as process.argv[2].

teaching.text: When you run `node script.js hello world`, Node puts the arguments into `process.argv` — an array of strings.
`process.argv[0]` is always the path to Node itself. `process.argv[1]` is the path to your script. `process.argv[2]` is the first real argument the user typed.
Arguments are always strings. If you need a number, convert it with `Number()` or `parseInt()`.

lessons.task: Print whatever argument is passed as process.argv[2].
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why are process.argv[0] and process.argv[1] skipped? What would happen if they weren't?

lessons.title: 4. The path module
lessons.summary: Work with file paths in a way that works on any operating system.

activities.title: Building paths safely
activities.instruction: The `path` module helps you build file paths that work on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Never join paths with string concatenation — use `path.join()` instead.

activities.title: What does path.join do?
activities.question: What does `path.join('a', 'b', 'c.js')` return?
activities.explanation: path.join combines path segments with the correct separator for the current OS.

activities.title: Join two path segments
activities.instruction: Use path.join() to combine 'data' and 'users.json', then print the result.

teaching.text: The `path` module is a built-in Node.js module. You load it with `require('path')` — no installation needed.
`path.join()` takes any number of string arguments and combines them into one path, using the correct separator for the operating system.
Other useful path methods: `path.basename('/a/b.txt')` returns `'b.txt'`, `path.extname('file.js')` returns `'.js'`.

lessons.task: Use path.join() to combine 'data' and 'users.json', then print the result.
lessons.starterCode:
const path = require('path');

// Join 'data' and 'users.json' and print the result
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why can't you just use string concatenation like 'data' + '/' + 'users.json'?

lessons.title: 5. The os module
lessons.summary: Get information about the operating system.

activities.title: System information
activities.instruction: The `os` module gives you details about the operating system — platform, CPU info, memory, home directory, and more.

activities.title: What is os.platform()?
activities.question: What does `os.platform()` return on a Windows computer?
activities.explanation: os.platform() returns 'win32' on Windows, 'darwin' on macOS, and 'linux' on Linux.

activities.title: Print the OS platform and memory
activities.instruction: Print the OS platform and total memory using the os module.

teaching.text: The `os` module is another built-in module. Load it with `require('os')`.
`os.platform()` returns `'win32'`, `'darwin'` (macOS), or `'linux'`. `os.cpus()` returns an array of CPU info objects. `os.freemem()` returns free memory in bytes.
Other useful methods: `os.homedir()` returns your home directory, `os.uptime()` returns how long the system has been running.

lessons.task: Print the OS platform and total memory using the os module.
lessons.starterCode:
const os = require('os');

// Print the platform and total memory
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would you use os.platform() to make your code behave differently on different operating systems?

lessons.title: 6. Reading and writing files
lessons.summary: The file system module — read, write, and manage files.

activities.title: Synchronous file operations
activities.instruction: The `fs` module has both synchronous and asynchronous versions. Synchronous methods end with `Sync` and block until the operation finishes — simpler for scripts.

activities.title: Sync vs async
activities.question: What is the difference between `fs.readFile()` and `fs.readFileSync()`?
choices: readFileSync blocks the program until the file is read
activities.answer: readFileSync blocks the program until the file is read
activities.explanation: Sync methods block execution. Async methods return immediately and call a callback when done — better for servers but more complex.

activities.title: Write and read a file
activities.instruction: Write 'Node.js is fun' to a file called note.txt, then read it back and print the content.

teaching.text: The `fs` (file system) module lets you read and write files. It's one of the most important built-in Node.js modules.
`writeFileSync(path, data)` creates or overwrites a file. `readFileSync(path, 'utf8')` reads it as a string. The `'utf8'` argument tells Node to return text instead of raw bytes.
In real applications, use the async versions (`fs.readFile`, `fs.writeFile`) with callbacks or promises so your program doesn't freeze while waiting for disk I/O.

lessons.task: Write 'Node.js is fun' to a file called note.txt, then read it back and print the content.
lessons.starterCode:
const fs = require('fs');

// Write 'Node.js is fun' to note.txt, then read and print it
hints: fs.readFileSync('note.txt', 'utf8') returns the content as a string.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does readFileSync need 'utf8' as the second argument? What happens without it?

tracks.name: Modules & npm
tracks.description: How Node.js organizes code into modules and manages packages with npm.

lessons.title: 7. require() and modules
lessons.summary: Loading code from other files using CommonJS modules.

activities.title: Requiring a file
activities.instruction: `require()` loads code from another file. When you require a file, Node runs it and returns whatever that file exports.

activities.title: What gets exported?
activities.question: If math.js has `module.exports = { add }` and you `require('./math')`, what does the variable `math` contain?
choices: The entire math.js file as a string
An object with an `add` property (the function)
activities.answer: An object with an `add` property (the function)
activities.explanation: module.exports defines what require() returns. Here it's an object with the add function.

activities.title: Export and use a function
activities.instruction: Create a multiply function, export it with module.exports, then require it and call multiply(4, 5). Print the result.

teaching.text: Node.js uses the CommonJS module system. Every file is a module. You export things with `module.exports` and load them with `require()`.
The `./` in `require('./math')` means 'relative to the current file'. Without it, Node looks in the `node_modules` folder.
Each file gets its own scope — variables defined in one file aren't visible in another unless explicitly exported.

lessons.task: Create a multiply function, export it, require it, and print multiply(4, 5).
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does each file get its own scope? What problem does this solve?

lessons.title: 8. Exporting patterns
lessons.summary: Different ways to export functions, classes, and values.

activities.title: Export styles
activities.instruction: There are two main export styles: export an object with named properties, or export a single function/class directly.

activities.title: Which require() call?
activities.question: If a file does `module.exports = function greet(name) { ... }`, how do you use it?
activities.explanation: When you export a single function directly, require() returns that function — no destructuring needed.

activities.title: Export a class and use it
activities.instruction: Create a Timer class with a start() method that prints 'Timer started', export it, require it, and call start().

teaching.text: You can export anything: functions, objects, classes, arrays, or primitive values. The key is what you put on `module.exports`.
Named exports work best when a module provides multiple things. Default exports work best when a module provides one main thing.
You can also use `exports.name = value` as shorthand, but never reassign `exports` itself — always use `module.exports`.

lessons.task: Create a Timer class with start() that prints 'Timer started', export it, require it, and call start().
hints: const Timer = require('./timer'); const t = new Timer(); t.start();
lessons.reflectionPrompt: When would you use a default export versus named exports?

lessons.title: 9. Built-in modules
lessons.summary: Node.js ships with modules for common tasks — no installation needed.

activities.title: Common built-in modules
activities.instruction: Node.js includes many built-in modules. You don't need to install them — just `require()` them by name.
activities.example:
const path = require('path');   // file paths
const os = require('os');       // OS info
const fs = require('fs');       // file system
const url = require('url');     // URL parsing
const http = require('http');   // HTTP server

console.log(path.extname('app.js'));
// Output: .js

activities.title: Built-in vs installed
activities.question: Which of these requires `npm install`?
activities.explanation: fs and path are built-in — they come with Node.js. Express is a third-party package that must be installed with npm.

activities.title: Use three built-in modules
activities.instruction: Print the file extension of 'index.html' using path.extname(), the OS platform using os.platform(), and whether a file exists using fs.existsSync('package.json').

teaching.text: Node.js ships with dozens of built-in modules. The most commonly used ones are `fs`, `path`, `os`, `http`, `url`, `crypto`, and `events`.
Built-in modules use `require('name')` — no `./` prefix. Third-party packages also use `require('name')` but must be installed first.
Run `node -e "console.log(Object.keys(require('module').builtinModules))"` to see all built-in modules.

lessons.task: Print the extension of 'index.html', the OS platform, and whether 'package.json' exists.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does Node.js include so many built-in modules instead of making you install everything?

lessons.title: 10. package.json
lessons.summary: The manifest file that describes your Node.js project.

activities.title: Understanding package.json
activities.instruction: Every Node.js project has a `package.json` file. It stores the project name, version, dependencies, and scripts.

activities.title: What is dependencies?
activities.question: What does the `dependencies` field in package.json do?
choices: Lists files the project needs to run
Lists npm packages the project needs to run
Lists commands to run at startup
activities.answer: Lists npm packages the project needs to run
activities.explanation: dependencies lists the npm packages your project uses. When someone runs npm install, these packages are downloaded.

activities.title: Read package.json
activities.instruction: Use require() to load package.json and print the project name and version.

teaching.text: `package.json` is the manifest for a Node.js project. It tells npm (and other tools) everything about your project.
Key fields: `name` (project name), `version` (semver), `main` (entry point), `scripts` (commands), `dependencies` (packages your app needs).
Run `npm init` to create a package.json interactively, or `npm init -y` to accept all defaults.

lessons.task: Load package.json with require() and print the name and version.
lessons.starterCode: // Load package.json and print name and version
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why can you require() a JSON file directly? What does Node do with it?

lessons.title: 11. npm — installing packages
lessons.summary: The Node Package Manager — how to add third-party code to your project.

activities.title: Using npm
activities.instruction: npm (Node Package Manager) lets you install packages created by other developers. After installing, you can require() them in your code.

activities.title: Where do packages go?
activities.question: When you run `npm install express`, where does the code go?
choices: Into a node_modules folder in your project
activities.answer: Into a node_modules folder in your project
activities.explanation: npm downloads packages into the node_modules folder. The package.json records what's installed.

activities.title: Install and use a package
activities.instruction: Install the 'chalk' package with npm, then require it and print 'Hello' in green.

teaching.text: npm is the package manager that comes with Node.js. It has over 2 million packages — libraries for almost everything.
`npm install <name>` downloads the package into `node_modules/` and adds it to `package.json` dependencies. Other developers can then run `npm install` to get all the same packages.
Never commit the `node_modules` folder to git — it's huge. The `package.json` and `package-lock.json` files are enough to recreate it.

lessons.task: Install the 'chalk' package, require it, and print 'Hello' in green.
hints: chalk.green('Hello') wraps the text in green ANSI codes.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why should node_modules never be committed to git?

tracks.name: Server Basics
tracks.description: Build HTTP servers with the built-in http module and understand request/response.

lessons.title: 12. The http module
lessons.summary: Create a basic HTTP server with Node.js.

activities.title: Hello server
activities.instruction: The built-in `http` module can create a web server. `http.createServer()` takes a callback that runs for every incoming request.

activities.title: What does listen() do?
activities.question: What does `server.listen(3000)` do?
choices: Opens port 3000 and waits for incoming connections
activities.answer: Opens port 3000 and waits for incoming connections
activities.explanation: listen() binds the server to a port and starts listening for HTTP requests.

activities.title: Create a server that responds
activities.instruction: Create an HTTP server on port 3000 that responds with 'Hello from Node!'.

teaching.text: The `http` module is built into Node.js. You can create a web server in just a few lines — no frameworks needed.

`createServer()` takes a callback with two arguments: `req` (the incoming request) and `res` (the response you send back). `res.writeHead()` sets the status code and headers. `res.end()` sends the body and finishes the response.
Port 3000 is a common default for development servers. You can use any available port number.

lessons.task: Create an HTTP server on port 3000 that responds with 'Hello from Node!'.
lessons.starterCode:
const http = require('http');

// Create a server that responds with 'Hello from Node!'
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why does Node.js need a callback for each request instead of just writing code that runs once?

lessons.title: 13. Reading the request
lessons.summary: Inspect incoming requests — URL, method, and headers.

activities.title: Request details
activities.instruction: The `req` object tells you everything about the incoming request: the URL path, HTTP method, headers, and any data sent by the client.

activities.title: What is req.url?
activities.question: If a user visits `http://localhost:3000/about`, what is `req.url`?
activities.explanation: req.url is just the path portion — '/about'. It doesn't include the protocol, hostname, or port.

activities.title: Route based on URL
activities.instruction: Create a server that responds with 'Home page' when the URL is '/' and 'About page' when the URL is '/about'.

teaching.text: Every request has a URL path, an HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.), and headers. You read these from the `req` object.
`req.url` is the path (like `/` or `/about`). `req.method` is the HTTP method (`GET`, `POST`, etc.). `req.headers` is an object with all the request headers.
This is the foundation of routing — deciding what to send back based on the URL and method.

lessons.task: Create a server that responds with 'Home page' for '/' and 'About page' for '/about'.
hints: Use if (req.url === '/') to check the path.
res.end('Home page'); for the root, res.end('About page'); for /about.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What happens if a user visits a URL you didn't handle? How should you respond?

lessons.title: 14. Sending different responses
lessons.summary: Control status codes, headers, and response bodies.

activities.title: Status codes and headers
activities.instruction: You control the response with `res.writeHead()` (status code + headers) and `res.end()` (the body). Common status codes: 200 (OK), 404 (Not Found), 500 (Server Error).

activities.title: Content-Type matters
activities.question: Why is `Content-Type: application/json` important when sending JSON?
choices: It tells the browser to format the JSON nicely
It tells the client to parse the response as JSON, not plain text
activities.answer: It tells the client to parse the response as JSON, not plain text
activities.explanation: Content-Type tells the client what format the data is in. Without it, the client might treat JSON as plain text.

activities.title: Send a JSON response
activities.instruction: Create a server that responds to '/api' with a JSON object: { "status": "ok", "count": 42 }.

teaching.text: The response has three parts: status code, headers, and body. You set the status and headers with `writeHead()`, then send the body with `end()`.

res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' });
res.end(JSON.stringify({ message: 'Hello!' }));
Status codes tell the client what happened: `200` = OK, `301` = Redirect, `404` = Not Found, `500` = Server Error. The `Content-Type` header tells the client what format the body is in.
For JSON responses, always set `Content-Type: application/json` and use `JSON.stringify()` to convert your object to a string.

lessons.task: Create a server that responds to '/api' with { "status": "ok", "count": 42 } as JSON.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: Why do you need JSON.stringify() instead of just passing the object to res.end()?

lessons.title: 15. Events and EventEmitter
lessons.summary: Node.js is built on events — learn the EventEmitter pattern.

activities.title: Emitting and listening
activities.instruction: The `events` module provides `EventEmitter` — an object that can emit named events and call functions when they fire. This pattern is everywhere in Node.js.

activities.title: Order of events
activities.question: If you call `emit('data')` before `on('data', fn)`, what happens?
choices: The handler never runs for that emit
The handler runs on the next emit
activities.answer: The handler never runs for that emit
activities.explanation: Events are not queued. If you emit before anyone is listening, the event is lost.

activities.title: Create and use an emitter
activities.instruction: Create an EventEmitter, listen for a 'ready' event that prints 'System ready!', then emit it.

teaching.text: Many Node.js objects emit events: HTTP servers emit `'request'`, streams emit `'data'` and `'end'`, processes emit `'exit'`. Understanding events helps you work with all of them.
`on(event, callback)` registers a listener. `emit(event, ...args)` fires the event and calls all registered listeners with the arguments you pass.
The HTTP server you built earlier uses this pattern: `server.on('request', callback)` is the same as passing the callback to `createServer()`.

lessons.task: Create an EventEmitter, listen for 'ready' that prints 'System ready!', then emit it.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: How is the EventEmitter pattern different from just calling a function directly?

lessons.title: 16. Building a JSON API
lessons.summary: Combine everything — build a server that handles multiple routes and returns JSON.

activities.title: A simple API
activities.instruction: A real API uses different routes to return different data. Combine req.url, status codes, and JSON to build one.

activities.title: Route matching
activities.question: What happens when a user visits `/api/unknown`?
activities.explanation: Since '/api/unknown' is not a key in the data object, the response is undefined, so the server returns a 404.

activities.title: Add a route
activities.instruction: Add a '/api/time' route to the server that returns { "time": <current time as a string> }.

teaching.text: A JSON API is a server that accepts HTTP requests and returns JSON data. Each URL path (route) returns different information.
This is the foundation of every web API. Frameworks like Express build on this same pattern — they just make routing and response handling more convenient.
In a real API, you'd also handle POST, PUT, DELETE methods and parse request bodies. The http module gives you all the building blocks.

lessons.task: Add a '/api/time' route that returns { "time": <current time string> }.
hints: new Date().toLocaleTimeString() returns a time string.
Set data['/api/time'] to { time: new Date().toLocaleTimeString() }.
lessons.reflectionPrompt: What would you need to change to make this API handle POST requests with data from the client?
